content: Cinnamon, scientifically known as Cinnamomum verum and belonging to the family Lauraceae, is a small evergreen tree native to Sri Lanka and southern India. The tree typically grows to a height of about 2 feet. Its bark is highly valued as a spice due to its distinctive aroma. In India, it is commonly referred to as Daalchini. The tree produces greenish flowers arranged in panicles, which emit a characteristic odor. Its fruit is a small, purple berry approximately one centimeter in diameter, containing a single seed. The essential oil derived from cinnamon bark constitutes about 0.5 to 1% of its composition. This oil is extracted by pounding the bark, macerating it in seawater, and then distilling the mixture. The resulting oil is golden-yellow in color, with the characteristic cinnamon aroma and a very hot, aromatic taste. The pungent flavor and scent are attributed to cinnamic aldehyde (or cinnamaldehyde). As the oil ages and absorbs oxygen, it darkens in color and develops resinous compounds. The essential oil contains several chemical components, including ethyl cinnamate, eugenol, cinnamaldehyde, beta-caryophyllene, linalool, and methyl chavicol. The name cinnamon originates from the Greek word kinnámōmon, which itself is derived from Phoenician and Hebrew terms (qinnāmōn), ultimately tracing back to a Malaysian language. In Malay and Indonesian, kayu manis translates to sweet wood. History Cinnamon has been known since ancient times and was highly prized by early civilizations, often regarded as a gift suitable for monarchs and other powerful figures. It was imported to Egypt from China as early as 2000 BCE and is mentioned in the Bible, such as in Exodus 30:23, where Moses is instructed to use sweet cinnamon (qinnāmōn) and cassia, and in Proverbs 7:17-18, where a lover's bed is perfumed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. Classical writers like Herodotus also referenced cinnamon. In ancient Rome, cinnamon was commonly used in funeral rites. Emperor Nero is said to have burned a year's supply of cinnamon at the funeral of his wife, Poppaea Sabina, in 65 CE. During the Middle Ages, the source of cinnamon was a closely guarded secret in the Western world. Arab traders transported the spice via overland routes to Alexandria, Egypt, where Venetian merchants monopolized its trade in Europe. The disruption of this trade by the rise of Mediterranean powers like the Mamluk Sultanate and the Ottoman Empire motivated Europeans to search for alternative routes to Asia. Portuguese traders discovered Ceylon (modern-day Sri Lanka) at the end of the 15th century and restructured cinnamon production through the local Salagama caste. They established a fort on the island in 1518 and maintained a monopoly on cinnamon for over a century. Dutch traders eventually ousted the Portuguese by allying with the inland Kandyan kingdom. The Dutch established a trading post in 1638, took control of cinnamon factories by 1640, and expelled the Portuguese entirely by 1658. A Dutch captain once remarked that the shores of the island were abundant with cinnamon, and its aroma could be detected eight leagues out to sea. The Dutch East India Company refined cinnamon harvesting methods and began cultivating their own trees. The British took control of the island from the Dutch in 1796. However, by this time, the monopoly on Ceylon cinnamon was declining due to the spread of cinnamon cultivation to other regions, the increasing acceptance of cassia bark as a substitute, and the rising popularity of commodities like coffee, tea, sugar, and chocolate. According to the FAO, Indonesia produced nearly 40% of the world's cinnamon output in 2005, followed by China, India, and Vietnam. Cultivation Cinnamon is harvested by growing the tree for two years and then coppicing it. The following year, multiple shoots sprout from the roots. These shoots are stripped of their bark, which is then left to dry. Only the thin inner bark, measuring about 0.5 millimeters, is used. The outer woody layer is removed, leaving meter-long strips of cinnamon that curl into rolls, or quills, as they dry. Each dried quill consists of strips from multiple shoots packed together. These quills are then cut into 5-10 centimeter pieces for sale. Cinnamon is primarily sourced from Sri Lanka but is also commercially grown in regions such as southern India (Tellicherry), Java, Sumatra, the West Indies, Brazil, Vietnam, Madagascar, Zanzibar, and Egypt. Sri Lankan cinnamon is characterized by its very thin, smooth bark, light yellowish-brown color, and highly fragrant aroma. Cinnamon and Cassia The term cinnamon is correctly used to refer to Ceylon cinnamon, also known as true cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum). However, related species like cassia (Cinnamomum aromaticum) and Cinnamomum burmannii are sometimes sold under the name cinnamon. Cassia is often labeled as Indonesian cinnamon or, in some cases, bastard cinnamon. True cinnamon, made from the thin inner bark, has a finer, less dense, and more crumbly texture and is considered milder than cassia. Cassia, on the other hand, is harder, woody, and thicker (2-3 millimeters), as it includes all layers of the bark. In the United States, most powdered cinnamon sold in supermarkets is actually cassia. True cinnamon is typically available only in stick form. European health agencies have warned against consuming large amounts of cassia due to its high coumarin content, a compound known to cause liver and kidney damage in high concentrations. Ceylon cinnamon and Cinnamomum burmannii contain much lower levels of coumarin. Whole cinnamon and cassia barks are easily distinguishable, and their microscopic characteristics are also distinct. Cinnamon sticks (quills) consist of many thin layers and can be easily ground into powder, whereas cassia sticks are much harder and can damage grinders. Powdered cinnamon and cassia are more difficult to differentiate. When treated with iodine tincture (a test for starch), pure cinnamon shows little reaction, while cassia produces a deep-blue tint, with the intensity depending on the proportion of cassia present. Cinnamon is sometimes confused with Cinnamomum tamala (Malabathrum) and Cinnamomum loureiroi (Saigon cinnamon). Uses Cinnamon bark is widely used as a spice, primarily as a condiment and flavoring agent in cooking. It is commonly used in desserts, chocolate, spicy candies, tea, hot cocoa, and liqueurs. In Middle Eastern cuisine, it is often added to savory dishes featuring chicken and lamb. In the United States, cinnamon is frequently combined with sugar to flavor cereals, bread-based dishes, and fruits, especially apples. Pre-mixed cinnamon-sugar blends are even sold for this purpose. Cinnamon is also used in pickling and is one of the few spices that can be consumed directly. In medicine, cinnamon has been traditionally used for its volatile oils and was once believed to cure colds. It has also been employed to treat diarrhea and other digestive issues. Cinnamon is high in antioxidant activity and has demonstrated antimicrobial properties, which aid in food preservation. Media reports have highlighted its potential pharmacological effects in managing type II diabetes, though the plant material studied was cassia rather than true cinnamon. Cinnamon has also been traditionally used to treat toothaches, combat bad breath, and promote digestion. Regular use is believed to stave off common colds. Additionally, cinnamon is used in Thelemic magick for invoking Apollo, as described in Aleister Crowley's Liber 777. It also serves as an insect repellent.
